web_title: 5. Management Promises, Plant Timelines & the KPIs That Matter
question: Which numbers should you track, and have the promises made so far been kept on time?

epigraph.quote: Our Mambattu facility in Andhra Pradesh is progressing as planned and we expect it to commence operation by end of the year.
epigraph.author: Stallion Q1 FY27 earnings call transcript, 17 August 2026 [8]

web_blocks.html: A management team makes promises in two currencies, turnover and dates. This chapter tracks both. It starts with six numbers you can check each quarter, then audits every dated promise the sources let me verify. The record is short, so the verdicts are provisional, and the gaps are stated where they matter.
The scorecard below uses only what the filings and calls state. Where management gave no target, the table says so rather than inventing one.

web_blocks.takeaway: Three of the six have a target and a reading that can be compared today. The customer-share line needs a current filing, and the commissioning dates are the test that arrives first.

web_blocks.title: What management promised, and what the record shows

web_blocks.html: The record is short. The October 2025 call is the earliest dated set of promises I could verify, and the August 2026 call is the latest. Between them they make five checkable claims. The table audits each one.

web_blocks.takeaway: One promise was kept on time, two were moved, one changed its funding route, and one cannot be judged yet. The Khalapur verdict will be settled by its first quarterly results.

web_blocks.html: The gap matters as much as the verdicts. The RHP set aside ₹29.16 crore for the Khalapur specialty-gas facility and ₹21.18 crore for Mambattu from the offer [5]. Those are committed sums, but the sources I checked give them no completion dates. So for most of the committed money, there is no dated promise to audit. Treat that absence as a gap in the record, not as evidence that the timelines are sound.

web_blocks.title: The plant timelines, one at a time

web_blocks.html: The Bhilwara R-32 plant is the most important date in the record, because the company’s main product depends on it. In October 2025 management said: “we will ensure that within 9 months, we are up and running.” [10] In August 2026 the completion target was the end of December 2026 [9]. Asked on the August call why the plant had moved, management blamed the funding route. A planned preferential issue was dropped, and the rights issue reached the market only in February. Management said: “So what was originally planned to be December startup ended up being a March end startup.” [8] That remark conflicts with the end-December target given on the same call, and the sources do not reconcile the two.

Khalapur helium had a December 2025 expectation in October 2025: “we would expect that by December end, we should be operational in the Khalapur facility.” [10] In August 2026 management said commercial operations would begin in the coming quarter [9]. The Mambattu blend plant was said to start by the end of the year in August 2026 [8]. Neither of those two dates has come due, so they are open rather than missed.

web_blocks.title: The revenue guidance, put in numbers

web_blocks.html: Management said on the August call that it maintained guidance of 30% to 35% revenue growth a year for the next three years [9]. Start from FY26 revenue of ₹430.68 crore [1]. Three years at 30% gives about ₹946 crore by FY29. Three years at 35% gives about ₹1,060 crore. That is the range the guidance implies, and it is a long way from FY26.

Management also gave a peak. Asked about FY28, the company said revenue would be “Exceeding 1100 crores” once the helium, R-32 and Mambattu plants were all running [9]. From FY26, that peak needs growth of about 60% a year over two years, which is steeper than the three-year guidance. The same call said the Mambattu plant would add only about 10% to turnover at first [9]. Both statements can be true, but they are not the same growth path, and you should ask which one the company is planning on.

Management was also asked whether the FY27 contribution of about ₹250 crore from the R-32 plant still held. It answered: “It would change a little bit.” [9] That is an honest answer, and it moves the number in the direction you would expect. Keep the change in the record for the next quarter.

web_blocks.title: The September 2026 quarter, and management’s own caution

web_blocks.html: The September 2026 quarter is the lowest operating margin in the ten-quarter Screener series. Sales were ₹136.03 crore, but the operating margin was 2.20% and net profit was ₹2.45 crore [14]. Other income of ₹3.34 crore was larger than operating profit of about ₹2.99 crore, and the tax rate for the quarter was 57.22% [14]. Management had described the June quarter as a special quarter. On the August call it said: “Those are not the actual numbers at our current business level that we enjoy. So how much of it continues I have no idea.” [8]

I did not find a management explanation for the September 2026 quarter in the sources. Until one is published, treat the quarter as unexplained. The honest reading is that the margin was very strong in June, weak in September, and the company itself does not yet know which level is the run-rate.

web_blocks.company: Olin Corporation (United States, Chlor Alkali Products and Vinyls segment)
web_blocks.region_era: United States, 2022 to 2023, chlor-alkali and vinyls commodity cycle
web_blocks.mechanism: A commodity-spread segment lost profit faster than sales in a single year, as volumes and selling rates fell together. The fourth-quarter margin fell by about two-thirds.
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: Segment income before taxes fell from $1,181.3 million in 2022 to $664.2 million in 2023 on sales of $5,085.0 million and $3,995.1 million, a margin of about 23% falling to about 17% [30]. Fourth-quarter segment earnings fell from $252.3 million on $1,172.8 million of sales to $65.9 million on $906.1 million, a margin of about 21.5% falling to about 7.3% [31].
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: Judge a commodity earnings base by its trough margin, not its peak. Stallion’s own EBITDA margin fell from 17.71% to 6.90% in one year [7], so a strong year is not a floor for earnings or for what a buyer should pay for them.

web_blocks.html: This is only half of the Olin case. How the market re-rated the company as its margin fell is not quantified here, because this blind pass leaves out market data. The annual figure is income before taxes and the quarterly figure is segment earnings, so the two are close but not identical measures. The filings show the margin fall; the re-rating is left open.

web_blocks.title: NARRATOR’S REFLECTION
paragraphs: Pick one date and watch it. Bhilwara has already moved once, from July to December 2026, and the same call carried a “March end startup” remark. The first time a company moves a date, it is a note. The second time, it is a pattern. Keep the list of dates on your desk and cross them off as each one is met or missed.

Then watch the margin against the mix. A strong quarter that management calls special is not yet evidence of a new level, and a weak quarter is not yet evidence of collapse. The next two quarters will tell you which one this is.

book_paragraphs: Now let us test the promises. A management team can make two kinds of promise: a number, such as turnover or profit, and a date, such as when a plant will run. Dates are easier to check, because they either happen or they do not. In this chapter I track both, with the record I could verify, and I try to say where the record is thin.

The earliest dated set of promises I could verify comes from the October 2025 call. Management said it expected FY26 turnover of about 430 crore and profit after tax of about 40 crore. The audited accounts came in at 430.68 crore and 43.84 crore. That is a promise kept, and you should say so plainly. A management team that keeps one promise deserves a hearing on the next one, but not a free pass.

The next promise is the one that matters most. In October 2025 management said the R-32 plant at Bhilwara would be up and running within nine months, which meant July 2026. By August 2026 the target was the end of December. On the same August call, management also described the start as a March-end startup. Those are two different remarks about one plant, and the sources do not reconcile them. When a plant is the reason the company’s main product matters, a two-quarter slip with an unreconciled second date is the thing to watch.

Management blamed the slip on the funding route. The company had planned a preferential share issue, the plan fell away, and the rights issue reached the market only in February. Funding came late, so the work started late. That is a plausible account, and it is also an account that changes the October promise. In October management said the Bhilwara funding came from internal accruals. In August it described a route that was not internal accruals at all. You should notice the change, even if the reason behind it is reasonable.

Khalapur is the next test. In October 2025 management expected the Khalapur facility to be operational by the end of December. In August 2026 it said commercial operations would start in the coming quarter. That is not yet a missed date. It is a date that is still open, and the first quarterly result will show whether it was met. The Mambattu blend plant has a similar open date, the end of 2026. Neither has come due.

Look at the revenue guidance as arithmetic. Start from FY26 revenue of about 431 crore. Growth of 30 percent a year for three years gets you to about 946 crore by FY29. At 35 percent a year, you reach about 1,060 crore. Then management gave a peak for FY28 of more than 1,100 crore. Reaching that by FY28 means growth of about 60 percent a year from FY26, which is far steeper than the three-year guidance. Both figures came from the same call. You cannot plan on both, and you should ask management which one it is planning on.

The September 2026 quarter is the most recent data point, and it is weak. Sales were up almost 29 percent on a year earlier, yet the operating margin was about 2 percent, and net profit was about 2.5 crore. Other income was bigger than operating profit. The tax rate was above 57 percent. Management had called June a special quarter, and it said the June numbers were not what the business would deliver at its current level. I did not find a management explanation for September. Until one is published, treat the quarter as unexplained rather than as a new trend.

So what is the practical rule? Track six numbers each quarter: revenue growth, operating margin, net profit, the plant dates, customer concentration, and cash conversion. Keep a list of dated promises, cross each one off as it is met or missed, and count the misses. One slip is a note. Two slips on the same plant are a pattern. And a single strong quarter, however it is described, is not yet a new level of profit.

Look at the Mambattu line before you accept it. Management said the plant would start by the end of 2026, and that it may not add much more than about 10 percent to turnover at first. That is a modest claim, and modest claims are easier to keep. Treat it as a check on the company’s ambition rather than as a driver of growth, and look for the first quarter in which the plant’s contribution shows up on its own.

Keep the promise audit honest in both directions. One promise was kept: the FY26 turnover and profit figures came in where management said they would. That deserves credit. But the two plant dates carry most of the company’s future, and both have moved or are still open. A management team that is right about the smaller numbers and late on the larger dates is telling you where its planning is strongest and where it is weakest.

When you read a quarter, check it in a fixed order. Start with what the company said it would deliver, then check the margin, then the profit, and only then the growth rate. Growth is the easiest figure to report well. The margin is the figure that shows whether the growth was worth having. The September quarter had strong growth and a very weak margin, which is the order in which you should read it.

The committed money deserves its own line on your list. The offer document of January 2025 set aside 29.16 crore for the Khalapur specialty-gas facility and 21.18 crore for Mambattu. The sources I read give those sums no completion dates. When the plants come online, check whether the money went to the plant it was set aside for. That is a simple check, and it is one the record does not yet let you make.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR’S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Write down the one date you care about most, and the day you will check it. If it slips once, note it. If it slips twice, change how much weight you give the next promise. A management team that keeps its dates earns trust slowly, and it loses that trust in a single missed quarter.
